context: The American job market your grandparents grew up understanding came with insurance, a pension, paid time off, and a predictable schedule. Underneath all of it sat a promise: decades of work would buy decades of stability, and the children raised on that stability would inherit something slightly better. Most employers have since withdrawn that arrangement from most jobs. The job now asks for availability across the whole day, retirement now self-funded, side income is needed to cover what the average wage doesn't, and the unpaid emotional labor is never accounted for by the employer.[^nirs-retirement] The conditions settled into a status quo. The demand keeps climbing as productivity increases. Workers pay those costs twice, first through flat wages and then through dysregulated sleep, attention, and health, and they pay it for years before understanding what it's costing them.

context: Then there is the information environment, which has changed faster than any of them. A generation ago it consisted of two or three local newspapers, three national networks, public radio, a handful of magazines, and a few hours of news a day. Today the platform on an adult's phone adjusts what it shows that adult according to how they reacted to the last thing it showed them, and it tracks the reaction and updates the next item minute by minute. Now one handheld device mediates work, banking, calendars, relationships, news, dating, healthcare tracking, school portals, and increasingly, private conversations with AI systems that know you better than your friends.

context: Survival is the most immediate of the three forces. The nervous system runs a threat-response hierarchy, fight and flight and freeze and fawn, and those responses have kept human beings alive through danger for as long as there have been human beings.[^porges-polyvagal] A system organized around threat works from a shorter list of options, because a shorter list is faster, and speed is what threat rewards. Regulated, you can see a dozen moves. Threatened, you see only the handful of moves that once saved a life. The nervous system reads most environments correctly and spends as little time processing as it can. Once the danger passes, it is supposed to return to the longer list. Often it does not, and you keep operating from the short list for years, inside conditions that may no longer be dangerous, because the nervous system never received the repeated evidence it needs to widen the list again.

context: Reactive choosing finishes the pattern, and it starts before you are fully awake. The second the phone wakes, the messages are already waiting. Then the meeting request, then the news. By mid-morning, with the nervous system already lit, the feeds take over and hand you a steady supply of other people's outrage and other people's staged lives.[^zuboff-surveillance] Each item asks for a response, and most of them get one. From the outside, all that responding looks like a productive day. From the inside, it feels like a treadmill, where the work is real and the ground never moves. Answering well is a genuine skill, and it spends the same hours and attention that building something would have taken. A response also ends inside the day, which makes it register as progress, while the things you actually want out of a life have to be returned to again and again over months before they amount to anything. Those are the ones that keep getting postponed.

text: Trauma, burnout, and survival plasticity are three distinct phenomena that get used as if they're synonyms, and the confusion costs readers, clinicians, and institutions real understanding. Trauma is what a system does with an event or condition it couldn't process at the time. Burnout is what happens to a regulated system when demand outpaces recovery capacity over an extended period. Survival plasticity is the broader category underneath both: the adaptations a body makes to survive whatever conditions it's actually inside.
